detail: list secrets across all namespaces (GET /api/v1/secrets) succeeded

Triage this alert. Determine whether it is malicious, who or what is behind it, everything the actor did, and the full scope of impact across the company's payments-prod clusters. Separate malicious activity from benign lookalikes.
system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_enriched holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID), with context already joined onto every row in the `enrichment` struct: the person behind each principal (name, department, out-of-office, usual client OS and mismatch), service-account ownership and whether it called from outside its expected network, source IP reputation, asset classification, and for pod creates whether the workload is privileged, platform-allowlisted and from an approved registry. Tools search and summarize it directly; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

content.text: Clearly malicious. Let's see all activity from the attacker IP and any other principals.

input.summary: Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com) is on PTO from 10-12 to 10-19. His credentials were used from 198.51.100.23, a known-malicious address on NIGHTOWL-HOSTING (ASN 64511, NL, bulletproof VPS hosting with an open Docker registry on port 5000). The client was linux kubectl, but he normally uses darwin. The same attack ran in order on EKS (14:02–14:25), GKE (14:38–15:01) and AKS (15:11–15:34). On each cluster the attacker checked their own permissions and listed namespaces. Attempts to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job were denied. They then read payments-db-credentials and launched a privileged pod, debug-tools-7f9c, with hostPID and the node's root filesystem mounted. They exec'd into that pod. Shortly afterwards the argocd-application-controller service account (cluster-admin) was used from the attacker IP, outside its expected network, so its token was most likely stolen through the node. With it they listed clusterrolebindings and created 'jdoe-break-glass', which grants jdoe cluster-admin. With cluster-admin they set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet 'kube-metrics-agent' and a CronJob 'node-cert-rotate' (runs every 15 minutes), both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service 'metrics-agent-np' on port 30080. They finished with the cluster-wide secret listing that triggered the alert. All three PCI payments-prod clusters are fully compromised. I found no use of this infrastructure or these objects from any other IP.

With cluster-admin they set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet 'kube-metrics-agent' and a CronJob 'node-cert-rotate' (runs every 15 minutes), both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service 'metrics-agent-np' on port 30080. They finished with the cluster-wide secret listing that triggered the alert. All three PCI payments-prod clusters are fully compromised. I found no use of this infrastructure or these objects from any other IP.
